^xE05030--------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Cast When Damage Taken ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------^7
The core concept of the build is centered around the CWDT gem to automatically trigger spells via a damage taken feedback loop.
In order for this to work, we need to take a certain amount of damage from hits, also known as the "damage threshold" that you can find listed on the gem itself. This threshold increases as you level up the gem, which also automatically makes it increasingly more difficult to achieve the highest possible trigger rate.
Each spell linked to ^xE05030CWDT^7 gains a global cooldown that is shared across the same spells. I.e. Ice Spear and Ice Spear of Splitting will not work together if the cooldowns overlap. It's important to note that spells that are on cooldown will not track damage taken during this time. Damage tracked by supported spells resets upon visiting new areas (that have a loading screen) and can also be reset by unequipping the spell gem (unconfirmed).
There's a certain trigger order that dictates which spell will be triggered in which order, as shown here:
^xC8C8C8 (1)-->(2) | (4)<--(3) | (5)-->(6)
Body Armour -> Left ring -> Main Hand -> Right ring -> Off Hand -> Helmet -> Amulet -> Gloves -> Boots^7
In the above mentioned example, depending on where either Ice Spear is socketed, only the one in the higher trigger priority will be triggered first, applying the global cooldown and preventing the second copy from being triggered. As in, say you have regular ^x7070FFIce Spear^7 socketed in the body armour (1) and ^x7070FFIce Spear of Splitting^7 socketed in body armour (2), regular Ice Spear will always trigger first and go on cooldown, preventing the other from being triggered. To avoid any confusion: Yes, transfigured gems are considered the "same" gem but with altered mechanics.
It is technically possible to use multiple copies of the same skill, but only if they are socketed in other CWDT setups (section "^xE05030Staggered CWDT^7") and only if their cooldowns don't overlap. For this particular build, this is not feasible due to the maxed out trigger rate.
However, this trigger order is mainly only relevant assuming that all triggers are ready to fire at the same time, which they will not do in this build due to varying damage taken thresholds that take priority. (Because a spell cannot be triggered if the damage threshold is not met, regardless of trigger order.)
CWDT's base cooldown is 0.250 seconds, though in reality this ends up being 0.264 seconds due to server tick rate (during which it cannot update the cooldown state). Which is a known fact that PoB also respects in its "effective trigger rate" calculations.
These are the relevant % increased Cooldown Recovery Rate breakpoints for this build:
^xC8C8C8 0% -> 3.79 triggers per second ^xADAA47 9% -> 4.33 triggers per second 27% -> 5.05 triggers per second^7 ^xADAA47^xFFFF77 52% -> 6.06 triggers per second^7^7 ^xADAA47^x70FF70 90% -> 7.58 triggers per second^7^7 ^xB97123^xE05030153% -> 10.1 triggers per second^7^xE05030 (currently not possible)^7^7^7
The gem also has an inherent less damage multiplier for triggered spells that is more significant at lower gem levels. For example, a level 1 CWDT gem applies a 65% less Damage multiplier. This modifier affects ALL damage dealt by supported spells.
Spells supported by CWDT have a maximum level before they stop being triggered. Said level is equal to the level requirement of the CWDT gem. I.e. a lvl 1 CWDT gem has a level requirement of 38, thus it can only support spells that require up to level (38), for example a level 1 (12) up to level 8 (38) ^x7070FFBlazing Salvo^7 gem.
Refer to section "^x8888FFSpells and added Damage^7" for additional information.
^xE05030---------------------------------------------------------------------------------^7 ^xE05030 Taking Damage ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------^7^7^7
The Damage Taken feedback loop is achieved via Eye of Innocence and igniting enemies with critical hits from Fire Damage (conveniently granted by Ngamahu's Sign). This ring is also used to counteract/balance out the self hit damage received, to make sure - at baseline and bare minimum - that our own triggers don't kill us immediately.
Every hit that ignites an enemy will deal a base ^xB97123100^7 ^xB97123Fire Damage^7 to us - ^xB97123120^7 with a 20% quality amulet - which translates into ^xB9712325-30^7 damage taken after 75% Fire Resistance. Same reason why you want to avoid -max res maps, if able.
Critical hits with Fire Damage inherently ignite, so we stack crit chance where possible to achieve 100% chance to crit, for guaranteed Ignites and critical hits for more damage. I recommend at least 80% crit chance to have this build function somewhat properly. This brings your chance to ignite to roughly 85% with non-crits included, which is what I would consider the minimum for this build.
Because this build requires Damage Taken to function, you cannot stack too much defense or damage reduction, as it will otherwise break the build. You can easily notice this in maps with a resistance shrine that kinda bricks the build.
^xE05030---------------------------------------------------------------------------------^7 ^xE05030 Staggered CWDT ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------^7^7^7
Because we are using a feedback loop in combination with cooldown spells, the proper technique is to use what I call "staggered CWDT" setups. By setup, I'm referring to each set of CWDT + linked spells in X item sockets.
CWDT lvl 1 has a damage threshold of 528. CWDT lvl 2 has a damage threshold of 583. CWDT lvl 3 has a damage threshold of 661. ...so on and so forth.
The way I do this is that I use multiple CWDT setups that are level (1), (2), (3), (4) and (5). Each spell that gets triggered (with some exceptions, i.e. ^x7070FFAssassin's Mark^7) will apply damage to us when it ignites and then feeds into the next tier's CWDT's damage counter. This creates that feedback loop that makes the build work the way it does.
As of version 3.28 Mirage Edition, I have further optimized this to a point I believe to be more or less optimal and more consistent overall, as it's practically impossible to test/adjust for every single micro variable.
Gem quality is absolutely crucial here - corrupted 23% quality gems specifically - to achieve an 11% lower damage threshold. For example, a lvl 1 23% CWDT gem has a damage threshold of 528 * 0.89 = 469 (rounded down), and 475 with 20% quality. This might not seem like much, but it makes a difference.
(Take note that you do not want to accidentally overlevel these gems as that cannot be reversed if corrupted. Make sure to keep track until they are leveled, then lock the gem levels and forget about it.)
Applying this to our current order of CWDT setups, we get a damage threshold (DT) of (with 23% quality gems):

Triggerbots for the doubled triggers. I chose to not further raise the tiers, as their DT scaling starts to increase quite a lot. For example, going from lvl 6 to lvl 7 CWDT (highest setup) has a DT of 892, which translates into a DT difference of +94. And it steadily increases. And if I were to shift the tiers to spread out the DT scaling, it starts to look even worse. For example, going from lvl 1 to lvl 3 CWDT has a DT difference of 119. Thus, the next best is, in fact, a lvl 2 CWDT. So on and so forth.
There's also a very valid reason why I use projectile spells: Not only because of their range advantage (and other mechanics they interact with), but because they have a travel time. This travel time is important to a degree because, remember, spells that are on cooldown cannot track damage taken.
^x8888FF--------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Spells and added Damage ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------^7
All skills have an ^xE05030^xB97123Added Damage Effectiveness^7^7 multiplier that dictates how much a skill benefits from added flat damage. They are generally balanced around this, so many multi-hit skills have lower values to compensate.
This is the entire driving force behind this build's damage potential. Because of the high damage penalty from CWDT, we can use sources of high flat damage to scale the base damage of supported spells to greater levels than they normally would have.
For example, a level 1 Fireball would have a base damage of ^xB971239-14 Fire Damage^7. The maximum supported spell level for a lvl 2-3 CWDT gem in this case would be a lvl 12 Fireball with a base damage of ^xB97123255-383^7 ^xB97123Fire Damage^7. But, because Fireball has a flat damage multiplier of 260% at gem level 1, we can make use of this via ^xAF6025The Burden of Shadows^7 to grant it a massive amount of base damage that vastly outpaces a level 12 gem. Of course, a lower level CWDT gem means a higher damage penalty as well, but we can get a lot more consistent damage and a significant increase in triggers per second this way.
And because gems generally also scale up in Mana Cost with levels, we can use this to add a lot of flat damage without the additional cost. This is why the build uses level 1 spells and added flat damage with high multipliers where possible.
^xD02090---------------------------------------------------------------------------------^7 ^xD02090Mechanical Significances^7^xD02090 & Interactions^7 ^xD02090---------------------------------------------------------------------------------^7
Certain spells, for example ^x7070FFSpark of the Nova^7 and ^x7070FFFireball^7, greatly benefit mechanically from sources of ^x70FF70Pierce^7. Spark's projectiles will be destroyed on hit by default, and Fireball will explode on impact by default. These behaviors can be changed with Pierce to allow Spark's projectiles to hit one more time (assuming they haven't expired yet) and Fireball's explosion to only occur on the final hit. Furthermore, this is required for the interaction with ^x70FF70Return^7, otherwise the projectiles would be destroyed on impact and unable to return. Meaning, for example, thanks to Pierce, Fireball can hit a boss, travel through it and not explode in its face, then return (assuming it has not hit anything else) and hit it again as it explodes. If not for Pierce, it would explode on impact and fail to return.
^xE05030Important to note ^7here^7^7, though, is that this can alter other projectiles to allow them to ^xE05030hit an enemy an additional time^7. For example, for projectiles that will not be destroyed, they can still return without a source of Pierce after hitting targets, but ^xE05030^7they ^7^xE05030cannot hit the same target again they are returning from^7^7. So, in order for this to work, the projectile has to be able to travel through the enemy and hit it again on its way back. Thus, ^x70FF70Pierce^7 is an essential part in the build and absolutely should not be skipped.
In general, this means that we can squeeze out more hits from projectile spells we use, which plays a vital role in how the build functions and performs, as I've explained in other sections.
Until you obtain a ^xE05030Vitality^7 ^xAF6025Watcher's Eye^7, you will not have access to ^x70FF70Pierce^7, as you will have to use ^xFFFF77Eldritch implicit gloves^7 to grant you ^xE05030Life Leech^7 from Chaos Damage. This is not the end of the world and the build will function just fine, it's just not very ideal.
^xE05030Knockback^7 is a very useful tool to have, especially in this build. It forcefully repositions an enemy when you hit them. This is a vital strategy to keep enemies at bay and potential melee damage away from you. The direction of the push depends on the relative position to the entity that applied the Knockback. Which in this case are the Triggerbots. Use this with strategical movement - by walking in front of the Triggerbots in a sweeping motion - to force enemies towards walls for bonus shotgunning. There are some enemies that cannot be knocked back (i.e. Shaper and Friends), but like 99% of the relevant ones can be pushed.
^x8888FFHinder^7 serves a similar purpose, except that it applies a movement slow. This is highly effective against charging enemy Rhoas, giving you more time to dodge their attacks. Other than that, I think it's self-explanatory.
^xAF6025--------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Triggerbots ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------^7
^x8888FF^x3F6DB3Triggerbots^7^7 not only double the amount of spells we can put out per second, but they are vital to the build, because, as I've described above, we need to meet certain damage thresholds per second to max out our trigger rate. At ^xC8C8C87.5 triggers per second^7, we need to (at least) take ^xC8C8C8469 * 7.5 ^xC8C8C8=^7^7 ^xE050303517^7 ^xE05030damage taken per second^7 to cap our lowest trigger rate. This can only happen when you have so many spell hits that you can take a ton of damage quickly.
Note: You do not have to double that number for the Triggerbots, as the damage taken dictates when the spells trigger, and they merely double that. Triggerbots do not multiply the damage taken required.
At base 14 projectile spells triggered in total, with 15 triggers per second, that's ^xC8C8C814 * 15^7^xC8C8C8 =^7 ^x8888FF210 spell casts per second^7. Assassin's Mark excluded. Not accounting for multi-hit spells and also not including returning projectiles, at ^xB9712330^7 self hit damage taken, that's already ^xC8C8C8210 * 30 =^7 ^xB97123^xE050306300 damage taken per second^7^7. The highest CWDT setup has a DT per second of ^xC8C8C8722 * 15 = ^xE050305415^7^7. So, once the loop is fully feeding into itself, the max trigger rate will be achieved within a few seconds (projectile travel time etc.), depending on how many enemies you hit.
Now, you might be reading this and thinking why wouldn't I increase the CWDT tiers even further, then? Because the napkin math above is simply the sustained (optimal) output. The spells have a cooldown timer during which they do not track damage taken. As you increase the threshold, the damage taken goes up, but we are lowering the cooldown timer even further. Meaning, as the spells go off cooldown, the projectiles are just returning and feeding into the DT again, triggering the spells in a row. When you increase this threshold, the spells might be off cooldown, but it takes more hits to trigger them again.
The result is that the build becomes stuttery and stops working properly, breaking the feedback loop, similar to when you get a max resist shrine buff and the loop is suddenly not working right. So, while the numbers work on paper, the reality is that not every single hit will always connect and align perfectly with the cooldowns. Thus, increasing the DT further is simply not a good idea.
In a similar fashion, as people have asked me about this a lot in the past: No, you cannot just make the build tankier. Damage Taken is tracked after damage mitigation. It's one of the caveats of this build that you learn to live with as you play it.
With ^x8888FF^x3F6DB3Triggerbots^7^7, every spell that damages us will do so twice (but also pay the cost twice when cast). This is the reason why I keep saying that this build would be be dead if Triggerbots were to be removed from the game. It just wouldn't be the same anyway.
I recommend speccing into them a bit later to avoid any issues with Recovery. If you take them too early, you will either be left with inconsistent casts due to a lack of Life/Mana, or die as a result.
^x7070FF^x3F6DB3---------------------------------------------------------------------------------^7^7 ^x3F6DB3 Scaling Damage^7^x7070FF ^x7070FF^x3F6DB3---------------------------------------------------------------------------------^7^7^7
Aside from all the flat damage, we need to scale our damage somehow. I opted for crit because I needed ^xB97123chance to ignite^7 anyway, and this was the best way of going about it. I've tried Elemental Overload (Elemental) variants in the past (with old versions of ^xAF6025Martyr of Innocence^7), and they are just not comparable to any crit based versions.
Furthermore, we make use of ^xD02090Wither^7 via ^xAF6025The Balance of Terror^7 to increase the Chaos Damage enemies take, and in addition to that we use the ^x3F6DB3Force of Darkness^7 and ^x3F6DB3Heart of Darkness^7 passives for Penetration. The ^x7070FFDespair^7 Curse is used to lower the enemy's Chaos resistance to basically zero (most of the relevant enemies have 30% base Chaos res). Sources of Chaos Penetration and Resistance Reduction (RR) are rather rare, so this and Wither is pretty much all we have access to.
A ^xAF6025Militant Faith^7 jewel with the ^xC8C8C8Dominus^7 roll adds the ^x3F6DB3Inner Conviction^7 keystone passive, which allows us to make use of our ^x8888FFPower Charges^7 to grant us more Spell Damage.
The build doesn't have a lot of sources of increased Damage, so it somewhat makes up for that with tattoos and a few passives, though any additional sources would add significant damage. Unfortunately, there's always some kind of tradeoff. For example, speccing into an additional jewel socket to allow for the use of ^xAF6025Replica Reckless Defence^7 for self Ignites via ^xAF6025Eye of Innocence^7 for the % increased Damage bonus is simply not feasible. The opportunity cost is far too high - even though the damage gain would be significant - as all the other jewels are uniques we need, and trading passives is not worth the loss in Life and Damage for what you get in return. For example, you would be trading ~7-8% more maximum Life for ~7% more Damage. I don't think that's worth it when more max HP means we can take more damage. The build has enough damage as is.
^x8888FF^x7070FFAssassin's Mark^7^7 is used to further raise the base crit chance of our spells against enemy targets. I highly recommend to use ^xFFFF77Eldritch rare boots^7 with ^x3F6DB3Brittle Ground^7 implicit until you aquire the ^xAF6025Forbidden^7 jewels^7^7.
^x3F6DB3Unnerve^7 on Hit from ^xFFFF77Eldritch implicit^7 on gloves makes enemies take increased Spell Damage, which is effectively additive with ^xD02090Wither^7 and other similar sources. At full stacks and while unnerved, the enemy takes 100% increased damage. Which is basically always the case because this build has so many hits per second.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Tips & Tricks ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
When you engage enemy packs, try to avoid walking into them in a straight line. That's a quick way back to your hideout. Instead, try and swerve around and into them, avoiding projectiles and causing melee enemies to chase you. Still, you will occasionally get one-tapped by stacked monster packs that hit you simultaneously. My number one cause of death, all the time, every time.
Also, be mindful of how and when you use your ^xAF6025Doedre's Elixir^7 or ^x7070FFForbidden Rite^7. What I like to do is pair it with a use of my life flask to help offset the initial damage taken. ^xADAA47Ward^7 is incredibly useful here, even if we don't have much.
Same applies to bosses. As the build uses returning projectiles, you have to swerve into them, then stay as close as possible and move around them in a swirling motion.
^x70FF70Never backtrack^7, if able. That's the golden rule of PoE; ^x70FF70always keep moving^7. Standing still for too long, or walking back into explosions or whatever, can easily get you killed. Such bullshit deaths get incredibly annoying past level 90. The way I do it is that I pay less attention to the mobs themselves and more attention to the ground. This way, I can spot volatiles much easier, though it can occasionally happen that you accidentally dash into some.
The loss of ^xC8C8C8Grafts^7 from the previous league is slightly irritating, as we now have to go back to a dual mod ^xAF6025Watcher's Eye^7 that is considerably more expensive, plus we lose access to ^xE05030^xB97123Endurance Charges^7^7. It's a minor hit to eHP, but a hit nonetheless.
If you keep dying, you could need more damage, or more levels for more crit. Yes, unironically. If too many enemies are alive for too long, you run a greater risk of getting killed. And the lower your DPS, the more lag you get in higher tier content, resulting in the same outcome. Besides, you absolutely need a high crit chance to heal quickly and to sustain the loop. I kept getting comments about this quite often, and it really boils down to this: If you don't crit, the build doesn't work and you die. It really is that simple.

As it stands, a base 1s interval that scales down to 0.8s is simply not enough. - The frogs initially take too long to come out and pop, which leaves you extremely vulnerable if you want to rely on these for damage.
They are really cool, though, especially because their explosions pack a punch and the spell does get doubled with Triggerbots. Sadly, mechanically speaking, it does not fit into PoE 1's gameplay loop. Promising skill, for sure. To be honest, the exploding frogs should just be a standalone skill. I would love to use it then, even as is. As it stands, though, requiring 2 sockets is a no-go, as maxed out frogs have roughly the DPS of a single low damage spell in this build.
A rare ^xFFFF77Mechanical Belt^7 is now replaced with the new ^xFFFF77Cord Belt^7 base. This allows for an additional anoint, which lets us allocate ^x3F6DB3Golem's Blood^7 for much needed regen and extra Life. You lose 1 spell this way, but it's not that big of a deal as it's only a minor DPS loss due to the added Life from the anoint (more Life = more damage).^7
I stopped using ^x70FF70Volatile Dead^7 because it mathematically no longer makes sense. The balls have a starting animation that lasts approximately 0.67 seconds, and they then have to move out and seek targets and explode. This wouldn't be a problem if not for the ^xB9712360 ball limit^7. The thing is, as we go up in trigger rate, the balls will never actually get a chance to explode, as they will be replaced before they hit anything. At 15 triggers per second (3.28 with 90% CDR), with 3 balls each, we can create 45 balls per second, yet barely half of them have even fully emerged. By the time the next casts are out, the balls will already be replaced before they reach the enemy. Thus, the only damaging part here would be the explosions themselves, but these do not scale well with this build.
In the past, I have made variants with AoE spells. While this is technically still very much a thing, especially with many of them having high damage effectiveness and near instant damage output, I simply do not consider this a viable strategy anymore. If you do want to explore this, though, I suggest you use spells such as ^x7070FF^x7070FF^x7070FF^7^x7070FFFirestorm of Meteors^7^7^7^7^7, ^x7070FFCrackling Lance of Branching^7, and so on.
